Allows the President to restrict imports that threaten to impair national security. The Commerce Department investigates and reports, and the President then decides whether to impose tariffs, quotas, or negotiated limits.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 76 Stat. 872](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/76/872){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 19 U.S.C. 1862](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/19/1862?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Investigation by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of Defense, within 270 days.
- Presidential decision on whether to 'adjust the imports' of the article.
- 'National security' is undefined and has been read to include the health of domestic industries.

## Why it matters

Little used for decades, it has been the basis for tariffs on steel, aluminum, automobiles, and other goods since 2018. It is the main example of national security language used as trade authority, and its importance grew after the limits placed on [IEEPA](ieepa-1977.qmd) in 2026.

## Current status

In force and heavily used. It was not affected by the Supreme Court's February 2026 ruling that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs.

## Where it sits

- **Layer.** Targeted provision. Single sections that grant a narrow authority, impose a condition, or require a report, often enacted in a defense authorization. Small in text, often decisive in practice. ([How the layers work](../study/index.qmd#the-authority-stack))
